title: Zoo of ideal Schauder bases: distinguishing ideals by simple ideal Schauder bases (Theorem 4.1)
author: Adam Kwela and Jaros{\l}aw Swaczyna
difficulty_reason: The counted theorem is the paper's distinguishing result and its proof is the technical core of the article's main section. Even with the paper's own prerequisites supplied as context - the definition of an ideal and of ideal convergence, of an I-Schauder basis, of the critical ideal CR(X,a-hat) and of a basis simple over another one (Definition def-simple) - the proof still has to build the witness basis: split the given infinite set E into consecutive intervals I_k, define the auxiliary quantities d_k as minima of norms of tails of the basis over each interval, define the perturbed vectors a_n (adding 2^n/d_k times a tail sum at the left endpoint of each interval) and the perturbed coordinate functionals a_n-star (subtracting 2^{b_k}/d_k times u_{b_k}-star on the shifted interval), verify the biorthogonality a_n-star(a_m) = delta_nm by hand, compute the exact difference of the partial-sum operators S_n(u-hat) - S_n(a-hat) as a cases* display, deduce the positive direction from E in I, and then, for E not in I, exhibit the single vector x = sum 2^{-n} u_n and show that the set of indices where the two partial-sum operators differ by at least 1 contains E, which is exactly what makes the perturbed family fail to be an I-Schauder basis. That is a constructive perturbation argument with a quantitative tail estimate, not a qualifying-examination exercise: it is the article's advertised mechanism for encoding an arbitrary infinite set into the critical ideal of a basis, which places the unit above ordinary PhD qualifying examinations: H3.
